subject: microbiology
title: Fungal Diagnostics: KOH Mount, Sabouraud Agar and Dimorphism

steps.tx: Microscopic bedside examination of clinical scrapings requires a **KOH mount** using ten to twenty percent potassium hydroxide solution. The strong alkali digests epidermal keratin, cellular debris, and host proteinaceous background while leaving fungal chitinous cell walls intact. Adding forty percent dimethyl sulfoxide accelerates clearing without requiring external thermal heating of the glass slide.
steps.say: Alkaline digestion clears opaque human keratin while fungal chitin walls survive.

vis.caption: Superficial fungal infection histopathology demonstrating branching septate fungal hyphae within the keratinised stratum corneum [Credit: CDC, StewardMD cleared]

steps.tx: Standard laboratory recovery of pathogenic fungi employs **Sabouraud dextrose agar** formulated with four percent dextrose and peptone at an acidic pH of 5.6. This low pH suppresses bacterial overgrowth while fostering fungal sporulation. Cycloheximide is added to inhibit saprophytic environmental moulds, while chloramphenicol prevents contaminating bacterial multiplication during prolonged multi-week incubation at twenty-five degrees Celsius.
steps.say: Acidic peptone-dextrose medium supports fungal mycelial growth while antibiotics suppress bacteria.

left.title: Medium composition
points: Four percent dextrose carbon source
One percent enzymatic digest peptone
Agar base adjusted to pH 5.6
Chloramphenicol antibacterial additive

right.title: Colony evaluation
points: Surface texture cottony, powdery, or glabrous
Colony colour and topography on obverse face
Diffusible pigment visible on reverse face
Incubation required for up to four weeks

steps.tx: Superficial lipid-dependent infection of the stratum corneum is caused by **Malassezia furfur**, a lipophilic yeast belonging to normal cutaneous microbiota. Overgrowth in sebaceous regions leads to pityriasis versicolor with hyperpigmented or hypopigmented macules. The organism requires exogenous fatty acid supplementation such as sterile olive oil overlay for successful in vitro growth on routine laboratory media.
steps.say: This lipophilic organism colonizes oily skin areas and demands fatty acids for culture.

nodes.label: Lipophilic yeast overgrowth in sebaceous gland areas
Production of azelaic acid inhibiting melanogenesis
Characteristic hypopigmented or fawn scaly macules

steps.tx: Direct microscopic examination of scales scraped from pityriasis versicolor demonstrates the pathognomonic **spaghetti and meatballs** pattern. Short, thick, curved, unbranched hyphal fragments represent the spaghetti elements, while clustered round budding yeast cells represent the meatballs. Staining scrapings with Albert stain or adding blue fountain pen ink enhances optical contrast under high-power light microscopy.
steps.say: Short curved hyphae interspersed with round yeast clusters resemble spaghetti with meatballs.

left.title: Spaghetti elements
points: Short, angular, stubby hyphal segments
Non-branching filament morphology
Thick cell walls with high refractility

right.title: Meatball elements
points: Clusters of spherical thick-walled yeast cells
Unipolar budding with collarette scar
Four to eight micrometre diameter spores

steps.tx: Systemic endemic mycoses are characterized biologically as **dimorphic fungi** that alter their morphological architecture depending on ambient temperature. At room temperature of twenty-five degrees Celsius in soil or nature, they grow as multicellular sporulating filamentous moulds. In animal or human host tissues at thirty-seven degrees Celsius, they convert entirely into unicellular pathogenic budding yeast.
steps.say: Dimorphic organisms grow as moulds in cool soil but convert into yeasts in warm mammalian tissue.

nodes.label: Saprophytic mould phase at 25 degrees Celsius with hyphae
Inhalation of airborne conidia into warm lung alveoli
Morphogenetic switch to yeast phase at 37 degrees Celsius

steps.tx: The cellular transformation between mould and yeast is driven by **thermal dimorphism** coupled with host nutritional cues and oxidative stress. Prototypic thermal dimorphic pathogens include Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, and Talaromyces marneffei. Coccidioides immitis represents a distinct variant that forms large endospore-filled spherules rather than simple budding yeasts in mammalian tissues.
steps.say: Temperature switching triggers gene expression altering cell wall carbohydrates and shape.

left.title: Yeast phase pathogens
points: Histoplasma intracellular small budding yeasts
Blastomyces broad-based thick-walled yeasts
Paracoccidioides mariner pilot-wheel budding yeasts
Talaromyces dividing by binary transverse fission

right.title: Spherule phase pathogen
points: Coccidioides forms large thick-walled spherules
Spherule diameter twenty to eighty micrometres
Internal cleavage into hundreds of endospores
Rupture releases endospores into tissue

steps.tx: Differentiating true dermatophytes from contaminant moulds requires assessing **dermatophyte test medium** containing phenol red indicator. Dermatophytes preferentially metabolize peptones first, producing alkaline amine metabolites that raise medium pH and turn the yellow agar bright red within days. Environmental saprophytic contaminants catabolize dextrose initially, generating acidic by-products that preserve the yellow color until carbohydrate depletion occurs.
steps.say: Dermatophytes produce alkaline amines from peptones that turn the indicator agar red.

left.title: Positive dermatophyte test
points: Rapid alkaline shift within three to seven days
Phenol red indicator converts from yellow to red
Concomitant growth of pale fuzzy aerial mycelia

right.title: Negative or saprophyte test
points: Agar remains yellow during early mycelial growth
Late color change only after sugar exhaustion
Heavily pigmented green, black, or grey moulds

steps.tx: Definitive microscopic identification of fungal cultures relies on mounting aerial mycelia in **lactophenol cotton blue**. Phenol acts as an immediate germicide killing live fungal elements, lactic acid preserves cellular morphology, and glycerol prevents preparation desiccation. Cotton blue dye, also called aniline blue, selectively stains fungal chitin and glucan intensely blue for high-contrast photomicrography.
steps.say: Lactophenol cotton blue fixes structures and stains chitinous fungal walls vivid blue.

nodes.label: Phenol component kills infectious spores instantly
Lactic acid clears and maintains osmotic architecture
Cotton blue dye binds chitin for crisp light microscopy
